The workflow software FireWorks together with the custodian job‑management tool automatically manages high‑throughput DFT calculations, self‑heals failed runs, and applies material‑type‑specific workflows.
Beyond‑DFT methods (HSE06, PBE0, G0W0, DMFT) are generated for a subset of materials to provide higher‑level reference data and enable uncertainty quantification.
JARVIS‑Tools implements automatic k‑point convergence protocols that improve the precision of DFT calculations.
Interpretability analyses of JARVIS‑ML models reveal physical insights that go beyond conventional materials‑science intuition.
The best one-step gradient-boosted tree regression model achieves 165±4 K MAE and 0.89 R² on the test set for melting temperature prediction.
Cohesive energy and elastic moduli (shear and bulk modulus) are the most important features for melting temperature prediction, as identified by both ensemble feature importance and SHAP analysis.
Models trained without elastic moduli features yield errors greater than 400 K, demonstrating that elastic features are necessary for accurate melting temperature predictions.

Tree ensemble methods (gradient-boosted trees and random forest regression) substantially outperform linear models, which achieve MAE >240 K and RMSE >340 K, at least 100 K worse than non-linear approaches.
The featurization methods are transferable to more complex compositions, enabling new ML models to be fitted without revising the materials embedding method given extended datasets.
None of the tested descriptors outperforms the others in terms of accuracy across all datasets.
Compressed models are 1x-10x faster than the original models for both training and inference.
NVNMD (non-von Neumann molecular dynamics) is 50x-100x faster than regular MD simulations.
FP32 precision is 0.5x to 2x faster than FP64 precision in nearly all tested systems while demonstrating similar validation errors.
DeePMD-kit APIs have been integrated into multiple third-party MD packages including LAMMPS, i-PI, GROMACS, AMBER, OpenMM, and ABACUS.
DeePMD-kit has added MPI implementation for multi-device training and MD simulations using Horovod for data-parallel distributed training.

Using the universal HamGNN model reduces computational cost by several orders of magnitude compared with DFT (e.g., 0.33 core·hours versus 181 core·hours for a large MOF) while preserving accuracy of band gaps and charge‑density differences.
MLIPs map atomic configurations to total energy and provide forces and stresses as analytical derivatives of the potential energy surface.
Approximately 40% of the UK's academic HPC was spent on DFT calculations in a recent year, most of which was AIMD.
Each cataloged DFT structure provides one energy and 3N forces (N = number of atoms) for training universal MLIPs.
MACE-MP0 performed best for discovering new stable materials with classification F1 score of 0.67, followed by CHGNet (0.61) and M3GNet (0.57).
DScribe provides a library of descriptors for machine learning in materials science.
Matminer is an open source toolkit for materials data mining.
MACE and grACE packages provide excellent scaling with number of elements while achieving high accuracy.
For MLIPs, the loss function is usually a weighted sum of RMSEs on forces and total energy.
There exists a continuum of approaches between pure PBPs (physics-derived with almost no fitting parameters) and pure MLIPs (purely numerical fit with almost no intuitive guidance).
MLIPs require substantial training data to learn the physics of the system, though this is becoming easier to meet as ab initio data becomes more plentiful and standardized.
MLIPs are straightforward to iteratively improve by adding more training data, whereas improving PBPs often requires fundamental changes to underlying functional forms.
U-MLIPs typically cover over 50 elements and may accurately model solids, liquids, and molecular structures.
First published U-MLIPs with broad periodic table applicability came nearly simultaneously in early 2022.
U-MLIPs generally have low energy and force errors compared to their ab initio training data.
Pre-relaxing hypothetical structures with U-MLIP before ab initio calculations resulted in approximately 3× time savings compared to running ab initio on un-relaxed structures.
Good agreement on target properties provides greater confidence in U-MLIP than just similar energies and forces on select structures.
MLIPs are not fundamentally limited to specific system types (metallic, ionic, reactive vs. nonreactive), unlike distinctions that were essential for PBPs.
Random cross-validation or k-fold CV are reasonable for test data if the data is not highly correlated.

U-MLIPs systematically underpredict energies and forces due to softening of the potential energy surface, attributed to biased sampling in training datasets from DFT ionic relaxations near local PES minima.
Some of the best-performing MLIPs are trained separately on energies and forces and are non-conservative, with forces not directly calculated by differentiating the PES.

Matbench v0.1 is a benchmark suite containing 13 supervised machine learning tasks (10 regression, 3 classification) for materials property prediction, with dataset sizes ranging from 312 to 132,752 samples.

Automatminer is a fully-automated machine learning pipeline consisting of four stages (autofeaturization, cleaning, dimensionality reduction, and AutoML search) that requires no user intervention or hyperparameter tuning.

Descriptor-based Automatminer and RF models have lower errors on small datasets but their improvement rates are shallower, with AutoML's advantage over conventional techniques narrowing as sample count increases and essentially lost near 10^5 samples.
All algorithms exhibit a universal trend of decreasing relative errors as dataset size increases.

For small datasets (<10^4 samples), inexpensive Automatminer presets (~1-5 minute training) retain the bulk of performance compared to expensive presets (24h+ training), with Express retaining 95% or more of the accuracy of more expensive presets at less than 50% of the computational cost on data-scarce tasks.

Matbench provides a consistent evaluation framework using five-fold nested cross-validation on identical folds across all algorithms to minimize comparison bias, with datasets pre-cleaned to remove unphysical computed data and task-irrelevant experimental data.
Automatminer source code and pre-processed Matbench tasks are open source and available online.
Using the IDNN reduces the computational cost of generating free‑energy data for continuum models by approximately two orders of magnitude compared with direct DFT sampling.

ML-based simulation can achieve comparable fidelity to direct numerical simulation while being considerably faster in computation time, with convolutional neural networks producing high-fidelity estimation of materials microstructure response with multiple orders of magnitude faster computation.
Trained ML models are typically only effective for interpolating data points and may not be reliable when extrapolating beyond the known data range.
Neural operators can make predictions that are not affected by discretization settings while maintaining prediction accuracy.
Physics-informed machine learning and transfer learning can reduce the need for large datasets while maintaining prediction accuracy and performance of ML models.
Physics-naïve ML architectures often fail to capture underlying physical laws despite having relatively high prediction performance.
Meta-learning allows ML algorithms to quickly learn and adapt to new tasks by leveraging experience from solving similar tasks with relatively small datasets.
ML can accelerate the solution of inverse problems by providing direct design solutions without requiring traditional iterative optimization processes.

Direct minimization of the total KS‑DFT energy with stochastic gradient descent reduces the asymptotic computational complexity from O(N⁴) to O(N³), and the full‑batch D4FT algorithm has complexity O(nN²)+O(n²N²), which is lower than the O(n²N²) complexity of conventional SCF; minibatch training further lowers the cost.
Across a benchmark set ranging from He to benzene, D4FT reproduces ground‑state energies of the reference PySCF implementation with deviations ≤0.02 Ha (LSDA/6‑31g and LSDA/STO‑3g).
D4FT correctly predicts the paramagnetic ground state of O₂ and the diamagnetic ground state of CO₂ by comparing spin‑restricted and spin‑unrestricted calculations.
D4FT successfully converges on unstable fullerene fragments (C₁₂₀, C₁₄₀) where PySCF fails to converge within the default iteration limit.
SevenNet achieves over 80% parallel efficiency in weak-scaling scenarios on a 32-GPU cluster with SiO2 benchmarks.
The melt-quench simulation with 112,000 atoms on 8 GPUs demonstrated 0.94 parallel efficiency compared to single-GPU baseline.
Architecture modifications reduced SevenNet-0 total model parameters from 16.24 million (GNoME) to 0.84 million.
SevenNet exhibits nearly ideal strong-scaling performance as long as GPUs are fully utilized.
Strong-scaling performance significantly declines with suboptimal GPU utilization, particularly for lightweight models or simulations with small numbers of atoms.
A 60-ps MD simulation with 112,000 atoms using SevenNet-0 required 12.7 hours, approximately 0.1 ns per day.
SevenNet interfaces with the LAMMPS package for MD simulations using TorchScript to integrate trained models.
For NASICON, training starting from FPMD configurations with 80 atoms fails to converge even after three training loops with activation energies spanning 0.2-0.4 eV.
For LLZO, results are quite insensitive to the choice of cell volume (NPT equilibrated vs experimental cif-file values) for producing the initial training set.

EquiformerV2+DeNS (a universal interatomic potential) achieves the highest classification performance among all evaluated models, with F1 scores up to 0.983, ROC AUC 0.96, and discovery acceleration factors up to 6.33, establishing state‑of‑the‑art for ML‑guided materials discovery.
Random‑forest models excel on small datasets but are outperformed by neural‑network models on large datasets due to the benefits of representation learning.
Models trained on Materials Project data systematically underpredict convex‑hull distances because the training set is biased toward low‑formation‑energy (stable) structures.
High disagreement among model predictions (large standard deviation) can be used to flag potential DFT relaxation failures in high‑throughput screenings.

GNoME achieves hit rates above 80% for structural predictions and 33% for composition-only predictions, compared to 1% in previous work, with active learning improving from less than 6% and 3% respectively over six rounds.
Previous machine-learning techniques have been ineffective in estimating material stability (decomposition energy) with respect to the convex hull.
Using a loss function with adaptive prefactors that emphasize forces early and energies/virial later reduces the total training time to a few core‑hours for all test cases.
Attention re-normalization improves energy MAE by 2.4% while force MAE remains approximately the same.
MACE uses four-body (higher-order) messages, allowing only two message‑passing layers to achieve converged accuracy, whereas prior equivariant MPNNs required five or six layers.

MACE shows superior extrapolation ability, reducing energy RMSE by about 30 % at 1200 K and 40 % on dihedral‑slice energies for the 3BPA benchmark, and achieving lower errors on geometries far from the training distribution.
On the 3BPA molecule energy profile, MACE predictions are closest to the DFT ground truth across three dihedral slices, outperforming BOTNet and NequIP.
Increasing the correlation order of messages (ν) steepens the learning‑curve power law, yielding higher data efficiency.
AFLOW can automatically calculate a wide suite of physical observables across a large database of structures with minimal human intervention.

AFLOW detects most calculation failures, automatically corrects input parameters, restarts calculations, and can run as a Unix daemon to generate, run, correct, and converge many DFT jobs per day, yielding higher throughput than manual management.
AFLOW implements DFT+U using the Dudarev formalism with default Ueff values for a wide range of elements.

DFT-based methods are practically limited to systems of a few hundred atoms, making generation of 8,000-atom amorphous carbon structures impossible with DFT-MD even on state-of-the-art supercomputers.

The training database includes liquid and amorphous structures, randomly distorted crystalline allotropes (diamond and graphite), and isolated dimer DFT data, extended iteratively by performing melt-quench simulations driven by previous GAP versions with DFT single-point computations for validation snapshots.
